Title: Slips, Trips, and Falls
Summary: Slips, trips, and falls are among the most common causes of workplace injuries, accounting for a significant portion of lost-time incidents every year. Most of these accidents are entirely preventable with awareness and good habits.
Key Points:
• Keep all walkways, aisles, and exits clear of clutter, cords, and debris
• Clean up spills immediately and post wet floor signs until the area is dry
• Wear footwear with adequate traction appropriate for your environment
• Use handrails on all stairways — every time, even on short flights
• Report any trip hazards, damaged flooring, or poor lighting to your supervisor
Did You Know Stat: Slips, trips, and falls cause 15% of all accidental workplace deaths and are the second leading cause of unintentional injury deaths overall. (OSHA)
Discussion Prompt: Can you identify one slip, trip, or fall hazard in your immediate work area right now?

Title: Stairway Safety
Summary: Stairways may feel routine, but they are a leading location for fall injuries — especially when people are distracted, carrying loads, or in a hurry. A few consistent habits eliminate most stairway incidents.
Key Points:
• Always use the handrail — treat it as non-negotiable, not optional
• Never carry loads that block your view of the steps ahead
• Walk at a controlled pace — rushing is the leading contributor to stairway falls
• Ensure adequate lighting; report burned-out bulbs immediately
• Keep stairs clear of stored items, tools, and trailing cords
Did You Know Stat: Stair and step injuries send over 1 million Americans to the ER each year. In workplaces, they are among the top 10 causes of lost-time injuries. (NIOSH)
Discussion Prompt: Do you always use the handrail on our stairways? What situations tempt you to skip it?

Title: Ladder Safety
Summary: Ladders are common equipment but account for hundreds of workplace fatalities and thousands of injuries annually. Proper setup, inspection, and use habits dramatically reduce risk.
Key Points:
• Inspect the ladder before each use — check for cracks, bent rungs, and missing feet
• Set a straight ladder at a 4:1 angle — one foot out for every four feet of height
• Maintain three points of contact (two hands, one foot — or two feet, one hand) at all times
• Never stand on the top two rungs of a step ladder or the top rung of a straight ladder
• Face the ladder when climbing or descending — never lean sideways beyond your belt buckle
Did You Know Stat: Falls from ladders account for approximately 300 worker fatalities and 164,000 emergency room-treated injuries each year in the U.S. (OSHA/CPSC)
Discussion Prompt: When did you last inspect a ladder before using it? What would you look for?

Title: Workplace Housekeeping
Summary: Good housekeeping is the foundation of workplace safety. A clean, organized work area reduces slips, trips, fire hazards, and stress — and reflects a culture where safety is taken seriously by everyone.
Key Points:
• Clean as you go — don't let debris, packaging, or spills accumulate during a task
• Maintain clear access to emergency equipment, electrical panels, and exits at all times
• Store materials properly — don't stack items where they could fall or block sightlines
• Dispose of waste and food scraps in designated containers to prevent pests and odors
• Good lighting is part of housekeeping — report burned-out bulbs and blocked windows
Did You Know Stat: Poor housekeeping is cited as a contributing factor in approximately 20% of all workplace injuries, even in cases where it isn't the primary cause. (OSHA)
Discussion Prompt: Look around your work area right now. What's one housekeeping improvement that could be made in the next 5 minutes?

Title: Parking Lot and Pedestrian Safety
Summary: Parking lots are one of the most overlooked workplace hazard zones. Vehicles, distracted drivers, poor lighting, and slippery surfaces combine to make them a frequent location for both vehicle incidents and pedestrian injuries.
Key Points:
• Stay off your phone while walking through parking lots — distracted walking is as dangerous as distracted driving
• Make eye contact with drivers before crossing in front of any vehicle
• Use marked pedestrian paths and crosswalks — don't cut between parked cars
• Be especially cautious in low-light conditions: dawn, dusk, and rainy or foggy days
• Report potholes, damaged pavement, and poor lighting to facilities management
Did You Know Stat: Approximately 60,000 pedestrians are injured in parking lot incidents annually in the U.S., and over 500 are killed. Many incidents involve distracted drivers or pedestrians. (NSC/NHTSA)
Discussion Prompt: Are you on your phone when you walk to or from your car? What hazards are in our specific parking area?

Title: Situational Awareness
Source Reference: OSHA General Duty Clause / DHS Ready.gov
Summary: Situational awareness means knowing what's happening around you — noticing what's normal and recognizing when something is off. It is the single most transferable safety skill there is, whether you're driving, walking, or working.
Key Points:
• Put your phone away when navigating unfamiliar, busy, or potentially hazardous environments
• When you enter a new space, take a few seconds to note exits, hazards, and anything unusual
• Trust your instincts — if something feels wrong, it may be worth acting on that feeling
• Avoid headphones in both ears in areas with vehicle or equipment traffic
• Check in on coworkers working alone or in remote areas — a quick call can be lifesaving
Did You Know Stat: Research consistently finds that distraction (particularly phone use) is a contributing factor in a growing proportion of workplace and pedestrian injuries. (NIOSH/CPSC)
Discussion Prompt: Can you think of a moment when something 'felt off' and you were right to pay attention? What did you notice?

Title: Office and Computer Ergonomics
Summary: Ergonomic injuries from office work develop gradually and are easy to ignore — until they become debilitating. Setting up your workstation correctly and taking short breaks can prevent months of discomfort.
Key Points:
• Position your monitor at arm's length, with the top of the screen at or just below eye level
• Keep your wrists flat and elbows at a 90-degree angle when typing — not bent up or down
• Adjust your chair so your feet are flat on the floor and thighs are roughly parallel to it
• Follow the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds
• Report early signs of discomfort — tingling, aching, stiffness — they're easier to address early
Did You Know Stat: Musculoskeletal disorders account for 33% of all worker injury and illness cases. Office workers are among the most affected groups. (BLS/OSHA)
Discussion Prompt: Is your current workstation set up ergonomically? When did you last adjust your monitor or chair height?

Title: Safe Lifting Techniques
Summary: Back injuries from improper lifting are one of the most common and costly workplace injuries. The good news: most are preventable with proper technique and by using the right tools for the job.
Key Points:
• Assess the load first — if it's too heavy or awkward, get help or use a cart
• Position yourself close to the load, feet shoulder-width apart for a stable base
• Bend at the knees and hips, not the waist — keep your back straight and core engaged
• Lift gradually using your leg muscles, keeping the load close to your body
• Never twist at the waist while carrying — pivot your whole body by moving your feet
Did You Know Stat: Back injuries account for nearly 20% of all workplace injuries and cost an estimated $50 billion in direct costs annually in the U.S. (OSHA/BLS)
Discussion Prompt: What is the heaviest object you regularly lift at work? Is there a cart or dolly available that you should be using?

Title: Repetitive Motion and Strain Injuries
Summary: Repetitive motion injuries build up over time from repeated small stresses on muscles, tendons, and nerves. They affect office workers, tradespeople, and everyone in between. Early recognition and intervention are key.
Key Points:
• Vary your tasks throughout the day to avoid prolonged use of the same muscle groups
• Keep wrists in a neutral (straight) position when performing repetitive tasks
• Stretch and take micro-breaks — even 30 seconds of rest between repetitive tasks reduces strain
• Use tools and equipment that minimize grip force and awkward joint positions
• Report symptoms early: tingling, numbness, weakness, or persistent aching are warning signs
Did You Know Stat: Carpal tunnel syndrome alone causes a median of 28 days away from work — more lost time than most other workplace injuries. (BLS)
Discussion Prompt: Does any part of your job involve repeated motions for extended periods? What changes could reduce that strain?

Title: Movement Breaks and Stretching
Summary: Extended periods of sitting or static posture — whether at a desk or standing in place — strain the body as much as heavy lifting. Regular movement is one of the simplest and most effective workplace health interventions.
Key Points:
• Stand up and move for at least 5 minutes every hour — set a reminder if needed
• Neck and shoulder rolls, wrist circles, and hip flexor stretches address the most common desk-worker tension points
• Standing desks are most beneficial when you alternate sitting and standing throughout the day — not standing all day
• A short walk at lunch significantly improves afternoon alertness and reduces musculoskeletal discomfort
• If your role requires prolonged standing, anti-fatigue mats and heel-to-toe weight shifting help reduce lower leg strain
Did You Know Stat: Prolonged sitting is associated with a 34% higher risk of all-cause mortality compared to minimal sitting, even after controlling for leisure-time physical activity. (CDC / Annals of Internal Medicine)
Discussion Prompt: How often do you get up from your workstation during a typical workday? What would make it easier to take more movement breaks?

Title: Eye Strain and Screen Fatigue
Summary: Computer vision syndrome (CVS) affects an estimated 75% of computer users. Symptoms — dry eyes, headache, blurred vision, and neck pain — are largely preventable with simple adjustments to your environment and habits.
Key Points:
• Follow the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something at least 20 feet away for 20 seconds
• Position your monitor about an arm's length away and slightly below eye level
• Reduce glare by positioning screens perpendicular to windows and using matte screen filters
• Blink consciously — screen users blink 66% less often, causing dryness and irritation
• Increase font size rather than leaning toward the screen — forward head posture adds significant neck strain
Did You Know Stat: Computer Vision Syndrome affects up to 90% of people who spend 3 or more hours per day at a computer. It accounts for a significant portion of eye-related occupational complaints. (AOA/NIOSH)
Discussion Prompt: Do you experience eye fatigue, headaches, or blurred vision at the end of a workday? When did you last have an eye exam?

Title: Fatigue and Workplace Safety
Summary: Fatigue is a significant but underrecognized workplace hazard. A fatigued worker has slower reaction times, reduced attention, and impaired judgment — comparable in some studies to being legally intoxicated.
Key Points:
• An adult needs 7-9 hours of sleep per night; consistently getting less creates a cumulative deficit
• Warning signs of dangerous fatigue: difficulty concentrating, microsleeps, irritability, slowed reaction time
• Never drive or operate equipment if you feel dangerously drowsy — speak up, it's a legitimate safety concern
• Caffeine delays fatigue but does not restore cognitive performance — it's not a substitute for sleep
• If your schedule or workload is consistently causing poor sleep, that's a systemic issue worth raising
Did You Know Stat: Fatigued workers are 70% more likely to be involved in accidents than well-rested workers. Fatigue contributes to an estimated 13% of workplace injuries. (NIOSH/NSC)
Discussion Prompt: Have you ever come to work seriously sleep-deprived? What tasks would you feel uncomfortable doing in that state?

Title: Heat Illness Prevention
Source Reference: OSHA-NIOSH Heat Safety Tool / General Duty Clause
Summary: Heat illness is entirely preventable — but it can progress from heat exhaustion to heat stroke in minutes, and heat stroke can be fatal if not treated immediately. Prevention is simple: water, rest, and shade.
Key Points:
• Drink water every 15-20 minutes during hot conditions, even if you don't feel thirsty
• New workers and those returning from time off need 7-14 days to acclimatize to heat
• Know the difference: heat exhaustion (heavy sweating, weakness, nausea) vs. heat stroke (no sweating, confusion — call 911 immediately)
• Buddy up in high heat — watch coworkers for signs of heat illness, which can impair self-awareness
• Check the heat index, not just temperature — humidity dramatically increases risk
Did You Know Stat: Heat is the leading cause of weather-related deaths in the U.S. Approximately 50-70 workers die from heat stroke each year in the workplace — nearly all preventable. (OSHA/NIOSH)
Discussion Prompt: What is the coolest place available to you during your shift in hot conditions? Does your whole team know the symptoms of heat stroke?

Title: Cold Weather Safety
Summary: Cold stress occurs when the body cannot maintain its normal temperature. Hypothermia and frostbite can develop faster than people expect — especially when wind, moisture, or exhaustion are involved.
Key Points:
• Dress in layers: moisture-wicking base layer, insulating middle layer, wind/water-resistant outer layer
• Keep dry — wet clothing loses 90% of its insulating value and accelerates heat loss
• Watch for hypothermia symptoms: uncontrollable shivering, confusion, slurred speech, loss of coordination
• For frostbite (white or grayish skin that is hard and numb), get to warmth immediately — do not rub the affected area
• Schedule warm breaks when working outdoors in cold conditions and limit continuous cold exposure
Did You Know Stat: Wind chill of -20°F can cause frostbite on exposed skin in 30 minutes or less. Adding wind to cold temperatures creates a dramatically more dangerous environment. (NOAA/OSHA)
Discussion Prompt: Do you have adequate warm clothing for the coldest conditions you'll work in this season? Is there a warm break area available?

Title: Sun Safety and UV Exposure
Source Reference: NIOSH Publication 2009-116 / CDC Skin Cancer Prevention
Summary: Skin cancer is the most common cancer in the United States, and outdoor workers have a significantly elevated risk from cumulative UV exposure. Simple habits reduce that risk substantially.
Key Points:
• Apply broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen to all exposed skin at least 15 minutes before going outdoors, and reapply every 2 hours
• Wear UV-protective clothing, a wide-brimmed hat, and UV-blocking sunglasses when working outdoors
• Seek shade during peak UV hours — typically 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.
• UV radiation penetrates clouds — overcast days still require sun protection
• Check your skin regularly for new or changing moles, spots, or lesions, and see a dermatologist annually
Did You Know Stat: Outdoor workers receive up to 3 times more UV radiation than indoor workers. One in five Americans will develop skin cancer by age 70. Early detection makes it highly treatable. (NIOSH/CDC)
Discussion Prompt: Do you apply sunscreen before outdoor work? Is sunscreen available as a facility supply for our outdoor team members?

Title: Hydration and Dehydration
Source Reference: NIOSH / CDC Workplace Health Resource Center
Summary: Dehydration impairs physical performance, cognitive function, and mood — often before you feel thirsty. Even mild dehydration has measurable effects on concentration and reaction time, which matters in any workplace.
Key Points:
• By the time you feel thirsty, you're likely already mildly dehydrated — drink water proactively throughout the day
• Aim for approximately 8 cups (64 oz) of water daily; more if working in heat or performing physical tasks
• Coffee, tea, and soft drinks contribute to hydration but shouldn't replace plain water
• Pale yellow urine indicates good hydration; dark yellow or amber signals you need to drink more
• Alcohol and high-caffeine energy drinks are diuretics and contribute to dehydration
Did You Know Stat: Even 1-2% dehydration (roughly 1.5 lbs for a 150-lb person) can reduce cognitive performance by up to 10% and significantly increase feelings of fatigue and irritability. (NIOSH/CDC)
Discussion Prompt: Do you drink water consistently throughout your workday, or do you rely on coffee and other beverages? Is clean water easily accessible in your work area?

Title: Mental Health in the Workplace
Source Reference: NIOSH Total Worker Health / CDC Workplace Mental Health
Summary: Mental health is a workplace safety issue. Stress, anxiety, and burnout impair decision-making, increase accident risk, and affect every person on a team. A workplace that takes mental health seriously has fewer injuries and better outcomes.
Key Points:
• Know the signs of burnout: emotional exhaustion, cynicism, reduced effectiveness, feeling detached from your work
• Employee Assistance Programs (EAPs) offer free, confidential counseling — if your workplace has one, it's worth knowing how to access it
• Managers play an outsized role in team mental health — how supervisors respond to stress signals matters enormously
• Social connection at work is a protective factor: checking in on coworkers reduces isolation
• Asking for help is a strength, not a weakness — and for safety-critical roles, speaking up when you're not okay is part of the job
Did You Know Stat: Depression and anxiety disorders cost the global economy an estimated $1 trillion per year in lost productivity. In the U.S., mental health conditions are a leading cause of disability leave. (WHO/NIOSH)
Discussion Prompt: Do you know how to access the EAP or mental health resources available through our organization? Would you feel comfortable using them?

Title: Workplace Stress and Burnout
Summary: Workplace stress is one of the leading causes of occupational illness in the United States. Chronic stress leads to burnout, physical health problems, and increased injury risk. Recognizing it early and taking action matters.
Key Points:
• Work-related stress causes include: excessive workload, lack of control, unclear roles, poor relationships, and fear of job insecurity
• Physical signs of chronic stress: persistent headaches, sleep problems, fatigue, muscle tension, digestive issues
• Short-term strategies: controlled breathing, brief physical movement, stepping away when frustrated
• Longer-term: set clear boundaries on after-hours work, talk to your supervisor about workload concerns
• Organizations can reduce stress by involving employees in decisions, clarifying expectations, and recognizing contributions
Did You Know Stat: According to NIOSH, 40% of workers report their job is 'very or extremely stressful.' Job stress costs U.S. employers more than $300 billion annually in absenteeism, diminished productivity, and healthcare costs. (NIOSH/APA)
Discussion Prompt: What is your most consistent source of work-related stress? Is it something that could be raised with a supervisor or addressed systemically?

Title: Hand Hygiene and Illness Prevention
Source Reference: NIOSH / CDC Hand Hygiene in Healthcare and Workplaces
Summary: Hand hygiene is one of the most effective public health interventions ever identified. In a workplace setting, it reduces illness transmission, sick days, and the spread of foodborne illnesses — all from a habit that takes 20 seconds.
Key Points:
• Wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds — that's about the time it takes to hum 'Happy Birthday' twice
• Critical handwashing moments: before eating, after using the restroom, after blowing your nose, after handling shared surfaces in high-traffic areas
• Hand sanitizer (60%+ alcohol) is effective when hands are not visibly soiled — but doesn't replace soap and water for all situations
• Avoid touching your eyes, nose, and mouth — viruses and bacteria enter through these mucous membranes
• Stay home when sick — coming in while ill is not dedication, it's a risk to your coworkers
Did You Know Stat: Regular handwashing can reduce the risk of respiratory illnesses like colds by 16-21% and diarrheal disease by 31%. Hands are the primary vector for most common illness transmission. (CDC)
Discussion Prompt: Are handwashing facilities or hand sanitizer easily accessible in your work area? Do we have a clear expectation about staying home when sick?

Title: Distracted Driving
Source Reference: OSHA Distracted Driving Initiative / FMCSA / NHTSA
Summary: Motor vehicle crashes are the leading cause of work-related deaths in the United States, and distraction — especially phone use — is a top contributing factor. No call, text, or email is worth a life.
Key Points:
• At 55 mph, looking at a phone for 5 seconds is the equivalent of driving the length of a football field with your eyes closed
• Hands-free devices are not significantly safer — the cognitive distraction is the primary hazard, not the hands
• Pull over completely and park before using a phone, even hands-free, for complex conversations
• Eating, adjusting GPS, and searching for items while driving are also forms of distraction
• Our workplace phone policy while driving applies even in personal vehicles during work-related travel
Did You Know Stat: Motor vehicle accidents are the #1 cause of occupational fatalities in the U.S., accounting for approximately 40% of all work-related deaths. (OSHA/BLS CFOI)
Discussion Prompt: Have you ever felt pressured to take a work call or check a message while driving? What should we do instead?

Title: Defensive Driving
Source Reference: OSHA 3120 Motor Vehicle Safety / NSC Defensive Driving
Summary: Defensive driving means anticipating hazards and having a plan before they become emergencies. It assumes other drivers will make mistakes — and prepares you to respond safely when they do.
Key Points:
• Maintain a following distance of at least 3-4 seconds in normal conditions; double it in rain, snow, or heavy traffic
• Scan 15-20 seconds ahead — anticipate, don't just react to what's directly in front of you
• Yield even when you have the right-of-way if another driver isn't going to stop
• Adjust speed for conditions — posted speed limits assume ideal conditions, not rain, fog, or ice
• Never drive aggressively in response to another driver's behavior — disengage and create space
Did You Know Stat: Defensive driving techniques could prevent or mitigate an estimated 90% of all traffic accidents, most of which are caused by human error rather than mechanical failure. (NHTSA)
Discussion Prompt: What is your following distance at highway speeds? Have you ever had to put your defensive driving skills to the test?

Title: Seatbelt Use
Summary: Seatbelts are the single most effective safety device ever installed in a vehicle. Yet thousands of people who die in vehicle crashes each year were not buckled up — including many on work-related trips.
Key Points:
• Seatbelts reduce the risk of death in a crash by 45% and serious injury by 50% — nothing else comes close
• The seatbelt must be worn correctly: lap belt across the hips (not abdomen), shoulder belt across the chest (not behind your back or under your arm)
• Seatbelt use is required by law in all 50 states — and required during all work-related vehicle travel
• Remind passengers to buckle up — driver accountability extends to everyone in the vehicle
• Short trips at low speeds account for a significant portion of serious accidents — don't skip the belt for a 'quick trip'
Did You Know Stat: In 2022, seatbelts saved an estimated 14,955 lives in the U.S. Of the occupants killed in crashes that year, 43% were not wearing a seatbelt. (NHTSA)
Discussion Prompt: Do you buckle up for every trip, including short ones? Do you remind passengers in your vehicle to buckle up?

Title: Work Travel Safety
Summary: Business travel introduces safety risks that many people underestimate — from unfamiliar roads and rental vehicles to hotel security and fatigue from time zone changes. A few habits substantially reduce that risk.
Key Points:
• Familiarize yourself with a rental vehicle's controls before leaving the lot — mirrors, wipers, headlights, and emergency brake
• Don't drive if you're significantly jet-lagged or fatigued — arrange for ground transportation instead
• Note emergency exits and stairwells when you check into a hotel; in a fire, elevators are unavailable
• Keep your hotel room number private in public areas and use the door deadbolt and chain when inside
• Share your travel itinerary with a colleague or family member, including hotel name and contact information
Did You Know Stat: Work-related road accidents are the most common cause of death among business travelers. Fatigue, unfamiliar vehicles, and unfamiliar roads are among the top contributing factors. (NSC/OSHA)
Discussion Prompt: When you travel for work, do you take precautions that you might skip at home? What's one habit you could add?

Title: Fire Extinguisher Use (PASS)
Summary: Knowing how to use a fire extinguisher — and when to use it versus when to evacuate — can prevent a small fire from becoming a catastrophic one. The PASS technique is universal and takes seconds to learn.
Key Points:
• PASS: Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle, Sweep side to side
• Only attempt to fight a fire if it is small, contained, you have an exit behind you, and you've activated the alarm first
• If the fire is larger than a trash can, evacuate immediately — don't try to fight it
• Check extinguishers monthly: pressure gauge in the green zone, pin intact, nozzle unobstructed
• Know where the nearest extinguisher is in your work area before you ever need it
Did You Know Stat: Portable fire extinguishers successfully stop fires in 80% of reported incidents when used properly. (NFPA)
Discussion Prompt: Where is the nearest fire extinguisher to where you're sitting right now? Do you know what class it is?

Title: Fire Evacuation Procedures
Summary: An effective evacuation plan means everyone gets out safely without confusion or delay. OSHA requires all workplaces to have an Emergency Action Plan — and employees need to know it before an emergency occurs.
Key Points:
• Know at least two exit routes from your work area — your primary exit may be blocked
• When the alarm sounds, stop what you're doing and exit immediately — don't collect belongings
• Close doors behind you as you leave to slow fire spread; do not lock them
• Proceed to your designated assembly area and report to your supervisor or headcount monitor
• Never re-enter the building until an authorized official gives the all-clear
Did You Know Stat: People who have mentally rehearsed an evacuation route exit significantly faster than those who haven't. Fatalities increase sharply when employees delay to retrieve personal belongings. (NFPA)
Discussion Prompt: If you had to evacuate right now, which door would you use? Do you know where the assembly area is?

Title: Carbon Monoxide Awareness
Source Reference: OSHA 29 CFR 1910 / CDC Carbon Monoxide Fact Sheet
Summary: Carbon monoxide (CO) is an odorless, colorless gas that can be fatal within minutes at high concentrations. It is produced by any fuel-burning equipment — including vehicles, generators, heaters, and power tools — and can accumulate in enclosed spaces without warning.
Key Points:
• Never run a generator, gas-powered tool, or vehicle in an enclosed or partially enclosed space — including garages, tents, or near open windows
• Symptoms of CO exposure: headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea, shortness of breath, confusion — often mistaken for the flu
• If you suspect CO exposure, get everyone out immediately, call 911, and do not re-enter
• CO detectors should be installed near sleeping areas and on every level of a building; test them monthly
• Proper ventilation is the primary defense when using combustion equipment indoors or in vehicles
Did You Know Stat: CO poisoning causes approximately 400 non-fire-related deaths and 20,000+ emergency room visits annually in the U.S. It is entirely preventable with detection and proper ventilation. (CDC/OSHA)
Discussion Prompt: Are there CO detectors in your workplace or home? Do you know the symptoms of CO exposure and what to do if you suspect it?

Title: Severe Weather Preparedness
Summary: Severe weather — tornadoes, lightning, flooding, high winds — can develop quickly. Having a clear plan means making decisions now, not during the storm when time is short and stress is high.
Key Points:
• Know your facility's designated shelter-in-place location for tornado or severe wind events — interior room, lowest level, away from windows
• Lightning: if you can hear thunder, you are within striking distance — seek shelter immediately
• Flooded roads: never drive through standing water — just 6 inches can knock a person down, 2 feet can float most vehicles
• Have a battery-powered weather radio or a reliable alert app — don't rely on windows or hearing sirens
• After a storm, watch for downed power lines, unstable structures, and flooded basements
Did You Know Stat: Lightning strikes kill an average of 20 workers per year in the U.S., with outdoor workers most at risk. Flooding is the deadliest weather hazard overall. (OSHA/NOAA)
Discussion Prompt: Do you know where to shelter in your facility during a tornado warning? Have you seen the severe weather section of the Emergency Action Plan?

Title: First Aid Preparedness
Summary: Workplace first aid is about doing the right thing in the critical minutes before emergency services arrive. Every workplace is required to have adequate first aid resources — knowing how to use them can save a life.
Key Points:
• Know where the nearest first aid kit is and that it is stocked — volunteer to check it quarterly
• Know who the designated first aid responders are and how to reach them quickly
• For severe bleeding: apply direct, firm pressure with a clean cloth and don't release it
• For cardiac arrest: call 911, start CPR immediately, and send someone for the AED
• Do not move an injured person unless leaving them in place creates immediate additional danger
Did You Know Stat: Early CPR and defibrillation within the first few minutes of cardiac arrest can double or triple survival rates. Every minute without CPR reduces survival by 7-10%. (AHA/OSHA)
Discussion Prompt: Do you know CPR? Where is the nearest AED in this building? Could you get to it and back in under 3 minutes?

Title: Recognizing and Responding to Allergic Reactions
Summary: Severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis) can become life-threatening within minutes. Knowing how to recognize the signs and what to do — including when and how to use an epinephrine auto-injector — can save a coworker's life.
Key Points:
• Mild allergic symptoms: hives, itching, runny nose, minor swelling — monitor closely and seek medical attention
• Anaphylaxis warning signs: throat tightening, difficulty breathing, rapid heartbeat, sudden drop in blood pressure, loss of consciousness — call 911 immediately
• Epinephrine (EpiPen) is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis — if the person has one, help them use it and call 911
• Common triggers: foods (peanuts, shellfish, tree nuts, dairy), insect stings, latex, and certain medications
• After using epinephrine, the person must go to an ER — the effects wear off and symptoms can return
Did You Know Stat: Anaphylaxis affects approximately 1 in 50 Americans. About 150-200 Americans die from food-induced anaphylaxis each year — most deaths could have been prevented with faster epinephrine administration. (NIOSH/AAAAI)
Discussion Prompt: Does anyone on your immediate team have a known severe allergy? Do you know where their EpiPen is and how to use it if they couldn't?

Title: Your Emergency Action Plan
Summary: An Emergency Action Plan (EAP) defines exactly what everyone should do in various emergencies. Knowing the plan before an emergency is what makes it effective — reading it for the first time during a crisis is too late.
Key Points:
• Know the emergency communication system: alarm sounds, PA announcements, and who initiates them
• Understand your role — are you an evacuation warden, a shelter monitor, a first aid responder, or an evacuee?
• Know the location of emergency equipment: fire extinguishers, AEDs, eyewash stations, and first aid kits
• The EAP must cover: fire, medical emergencies, severe weather, and workplace violence at minimum
• Ask your supervisor where the written EAP is kept — review it at least once a year
Did You Know Stat: OSHA estimates that 60% of businesses do not have an updated emergency action plan. Workplaces with practiced EAPs have significantly better outcomes in actual emergencies.
Discussion Prompt: Have you reviewed our Emergency Action Plan in the last year? Do you know your specific role in an emergency?

Title: Workplace Violence Prevention
Summary: Workplace violence — ranging from verbal threats to physical assault — affects nearly 2 million workers annually. Prevention depends on awareness, clear reporting channels, and a culture that takes early warning signs seriously.
Key Points:
• Workplace violence includes threats, verbal abuse, intimidation, and physical assault — not just extreme incidents
• Report early warning signs: escalating verbal conflict, threats (even 'jokes'), unexplained anger, or someone fixating on a coworker
• Trust your instincts — if an interaction feels threatening or unsafe, it's worth reporting
• Know your facility's threat reporting procedure and who to contact (supervisor, HR, security)
• De-escalation basics: stay calm, don't argue, give physical space, avoid cornering someone, and call for help rather than managing alone
Did You Know Stat: Workplace violence is the third leading cause of occupational fatalities in the U.S. and the leading cause for women in the workplace. About 2 million workers experience it annually. (OSHA/BLS)
Discussion Prompt: Do you know how to report a threat or concerning behavior in our workplace? Have you ever dismissed something as 'probably nothing' that still felt off?

Title: Active Threat Response (Run, Hide, Fight)
Source Reference: DHS Run Hide Fight / OSHA Active Shooter Guidance
Summary: The 'Run, Hide, Fight' framework is the federal standard response to an active threat scenario. Knowing these steps in advance — and having mentally rehearsed them — dramatically improves survival odds.
Key Points:
• RUN: If there is a safe escape route, leave immediately. Leave belongings behind. Keep your hands visible. Call 911 once you're safe.
• HIDE: If escape isn't possible, lock or barricade the door, turn off lights, silence phones, and stay quiet and out of sight
• FIGHT: Only as an absolute last resort when your life is in immediate danger — act with aggression and commit fully
• When law enforcement arrives: keep hands visible and empty, don't make sudden movements, follow all instructions
• Know at least two exits from your work area and the locations of rooms that can be secured from the inside
Did You Know Stat: The average active shooter event lasts 12 minutes; law enforcement typically arrives in about 18 minutes. What you do in those first minutes is what determines outcomes. (FBI/DHS)
Discussion Prompt: Could you quickly identify two exit routes from this room right now? Do you know which doors in your area can be locked from the inside?

Title: Near-Miss Reporting
Source Reference: OSHA Voluntary Protection Programs / Heinrich's Triangle
Summary: A near-miss is an incident where no one was injured — but could have been. Near-misses are the most valuable safety data a workplace has, because they reveal hazards before someone gets hurt. Reporting them is an act of leadership.
Key Points:
• Report every near-miss, no matter how minor it seems — the next similar event might have a very different outcome
• A healthy near-miss reporting culture is non-punitive — people report because they know it leads to improvement, not blame
• For every serious injury, there are an estimated 29 minor injuries and 300 near-misses involving the same type of hazard
• When you report a near-miss, follow up to confirm a corrective action was actually taken
• Organizations that track near-misses proactively have significantly fewer serious incidents
Did You Know Stat: Heinrich's Safety Triangle: for every 1 serious injury, there are approximately 29 minor injuries and 300 near-miss events involving the same hazard. Addressing near-misses prevents the serious ones. (OSHA / Heinrich)
Discussion Prompt: Have you experienced a near-miss in the last month that you didn't report? What made you hesitate?

Title: Why We Investigate Incidents
Summary: Incident investigation isn't about assigning blame — it's about understanding why something happened so it doesn't happen again. Effective investigation digs past 'human error' to find the underlying system failures that made the error likely.
Key Points:
• All incidents — injuries, near-misses, and property damage — should be investigated to find root causes
• Root cause analysis asks 'why?' repeatedly until you reach a systemic, fixable cause — not just 'the worker wasn't careful'
• Preserve the scene after an incident when possible: take photos, note conditions, identify witnesses before memories fade
• Corrective actions must be specific, assigned to an owner, and have a completion date
• Sharing findings with the team reinforces the non-punitive intent and spreads learning across the organization
Did You Know Stat: Over 80% of incident investigations that fail to prevent recurrence cited 'retraining the worker' as the sole corrective action — a response that rarely addresses the actual root cause. (OSHA/AIHA)
Discussion Prompt: The last incident in your area — was a root cause found and corrected, or was it closed as 'worker error'?

Title: Stop Work Authority
Source Reference: DOE Worker Safety and Health Program (10 CFR 851) / OSHA 11(c)
Summary: Every worker has the right and the responsibility to stop work when they believe a condition is unsafe. Stop Work Authority is not just a right — in organizations with strong safety cultures, it is an expectation.
Key Points:
• Anyone can invoke Stop Work Authority when they observe an imminent danger or potential serious injury
• Invoke it clearly: 'I am stopping this work because...' — state the specific hazard you observed
• Work must not resume until the safety concern has been evaluated and resolved by a supervisor or safety officer
• No retaliation for a good-faith use of Stop Work Authority is permitted — it is protected under OSHA 11(c)
• If you have ever felt you couldn't stop unsafe work without consequences, that is a cultural problem worth raising
Did You Know Stat: Organizations with strong Stop Work Authority cultures have significantly lower serious injury and fatality rates. The DOE mandates SWA across all contractor sites under 10 CFR 851. (DOE EFCOG/OSHA)
Discussion Prompt: Have you ever stopped work due to a safety concern? If not, what has held you back? Do you feel genuinely empowered to do so here?

Title: What Makes a Strong Safety Culture
Summary: The Department of Energy identified that most serious industrial accidents trace back to organizational and cultural failures, not just individual mistakes. A strong safety culture means safety is genuinely valued — not just displayed on a poster.
Key Points:
• Safety culture is shaped most by what supervisors and leaders actually do — not by what policies say
• A questioning attitude means workers at any level challenge unsafe assumptions and speak up when something doesn't look right
• Psychological safety — knowing you can raise a concern without retaliation — is a prerequisite for good safety reporting
• Measure culture by leading indicators (near-miss reports, hazard observations, participation) not just lagging ones (injury rates)
• Normalizing small problems ('we always do it this way') is how organizations drift toward serious accidents
Did You Know Stat: Post-incident analyses of major industrial disasters — Chernobyl, Texas City, Deepwater Horizon — consistently find cultural and organizational failures as primary causes, with individual error as a downstream symptom. (DOE/Columbia Accident Investigation Board)
Discussion Prompt: Would you feel comfortable raising a safety concern with your supervisor today without fear of it reflecting poorly on you?

Title: Human Performance and Error Prevention
Summary: Human error is normal — but serious consequences from human error are not inevitable. The DOE Human Performance program provides practical tools to catch errors before they become incidents, regardless of industry.
Key Points:
• Error-likely situations include: time pressure, distraction, unclear expectations, fatigue, and novel or unfamiliar tasks — these deserve extra caution
• Self-check (STAR): Stop, Think, Act, Review — a brief pause before a critical action catches most errors
• Peer checking: a second person independently verifies a critical step before it's taken
• Place-keeping: use a physical checklist and mark steps as completed — don't rely on memory alone for multi-step tasks
• When something doesn't look right, pause and verify — 'if in doubt, don't' is a legitimate and professional response
Did You Know Stat: Studies of industrial incidents find that human error is a contributing factor in over 80% of events — but that most of those errors were preceded by identifiable error-likely conditions that could have triggered a pause. (DOE/NRC)
Discussion Prompt: Can you think of a task in your job where a simple self-check or peer-check step would meaningfully reduce the risk of a costly error?

Title: Selecting and Using PPE
Summary: Personal Protective Equipment is your last line of defense — it doesn't eliminate hazards, it reduces consequences if something goes wrong. Selecting the right PPE for the actual hazard is just as important as wearing it at all.
Key Points:
• PPE selection must be based on a hazard assessment — not just habit or convenience
• PPE must fit properly to be effective; ill-fitting equipment provides false security
• Inspect PPE before each use — worn, cracked, or damaged equipment must be replaced, not used
• Wearing PPE does not authorize skipping engineering controls or safer work practices — it is the last resort, not the first
• Your employer is required to provide appropriate PPE at no cost to you
Did You Know Stat: In approximately 37% of workplace incidents resulting in injuries, the victim was not wearing appropriate PPE for the hazard present. (OSHA analysis)
Discussion Prompt: Is the PPE you use daily the right choice for the specific hazards you face? When did you last have a formal hazard assessment?

Title: Eye and Face Protection
Summary: Eye injuries are among the most preventable workplace injuries — and among the most regretted. The difference between a close call and a life-changing injury is often whether proper eye protection was worn.
Key Points:
• Safety glasses protect against impact; goggles protect against splashes and fine dust — use the right type for the hazard
• Safety glasses must meet ANSI Z87.1 standards — look for the Z87 marking on the lens or frame
• Side shields are required when there is a risk of flying debris from the side
• Contact lenses do not provide eye protection and can trap particles or chemicals against the eye
• Face shields must always be worn over safety glasses — not as a replacement for them
Did You Know Stat: About 2,000 workers in the U.S. sustain job-related eye injuries every day. 90% of those injuries could have been prevented with proper eye protection. (OSHA/Prevent Blindness)
Discussion Prompt: Are you wearing the correct type of eye protection for your specific tasks, or reaching for the same glasses purely out of habit?

Title: Hearing Protection
Summary: Noise-induced hearing loss is permanent and painless — it develops gradually, making it easy to ignore until significant damage has already occurred. Once hearing is lost, it cannot be restored.
Key Points:
• Hearing protection is required when noise levels reach or exceed 90 dBA averaged over 8 hours
• Earplugs must be inserted correctly to achieve their rated noise reduction — improper insertion can reduce effectiveness by 50%
• Earmuffs should seal completely around the ear — glasses, hair, or jewelry can break the seal
• Hearing protection must be used consistently — even a single loud unprotected exposure causes damage
• Ringing or muffling after a noise exposure is a warning sign that damage is occurring
Did You Know Stat: Approximately 22 million U.S. workers are exposed to potentially damaging noise each year. Noise-induced hearing loss is the most common occupational disease in the country. (NIOSH)
Discussion Prompt: Do you notice ringing in your ears after your shift or after certain tasks? Are you using hearing protection in all situations where it's needed?

Title: Hazard Communication Basics
Summary: If chemicals are present in your workplace — even common cleaners, lubricants, or office supplies — OSHA's Hazard Communication standard requires that you know what they are, what hazards they pose, and how to handle them safely.
Key Points:
• Every hazardous chemical must have a label and a Safety Data Sheet (SDS) accessible to employees
• GHS labels include a signal word (Danger or Warning), hazard pictograms, and precautionary statements
• Never remove or deface a chemical label; relabel immediately if a label is damaged
• Secondary containers (spray bottles, cups) must also be labeled with the chemical name and hazard information
• Know where SDSs are stored in your workplace — they're your reference in a spill or exposure emergency
Did You Know Stat: OSHA's Hazard Communication standard consistently ranks as the #1 or #2 most cited standard each year — indicating widespread non-compliance across all industries.
Discussion Prompt: If a chemical spilled in your work area right now, would you know where to find its Safety Data Sheet? Have you ever read one?

Title: Dangerous Chemical Combinations
Summary: Mixing common workplace or household cleaning chemicals can create toxic gases or violent reactions — sometimes instantly. Some of the most dangerous combinations involve products you'd find in any supply closet.
Key Points:
• Never mix bleach with ammonia-based cleaners — produces toxic chloramine gas
• Never mix bleach with acids (vinegar, toilet bowl cleaner, rust remover) — produces chlorine gas
• Never mix different drain cleaners or strong bases with acids — reactions can be violent and produce heat
• Read labels before combining any cleaning products — 'do not mix with other chemicals' is a common warning for good reason
• If you accidentally create a chemical reaction or see fumes, evacuate the area and call for help
Did You Know Stat: Unintentional chemical mixing incidents — particularly involving household and workplace cleaners — send tens of thousands of people to emergency rooms each year in the U.S. (CDC/Poison Control)
Discussion Prompt: Are you confident you know which cleaning products in your area cannot be combined? Does your team know what to do if a chemical reaction occurs?

Title: Chemical Spill Response
Summary: A quick, appropriate response to a chemical spill protects everyone nearby. The wrong response — or no response — can turn a manageable incident into a serious injury or regulatory violation.
Key Points:
• Identify the chemical before responding — check the label or SDS for spill response guidance
• Only clean up a spill if you are trained, have the right PPE, and the spill is within your scope of response
• For unknown chemicals, large spills, or anything producing fumes, isolate the area and call your safety team or emergency services
• Use appropriate absorbent materials — never paper towels or rags for solvent spills
• Report all spills, even small ones — they're important for tracking exposures and regulatory compliance
Did You Know Stat: Thousands of chemical spills occur in U.S. workplaces each year. Improper cleanup is a leading cause of secondary injuries to responders, not just the initial incident. (EPA/OSHA)
Discussion Prompt: Do you have a spill kit in your work area? Do you know where it is, what's in it, and which spills are within your scope to handle?

Title: Break Room and Food Safety
Source Reference: NIOSH / CDC Food Safety at Work / FDA
Summary: Foodborne illness affects 48 million Americans each year — many of those incidents trace back to shared spaces like office break rooms and kitchens. Simple habits prevent most cases.
Key Points:
• Refrigerate perishable foods within 2 hours of preparation; the danger zone is 40°F–140°F
• Label food in shared refrigerators with your name and date — and discard anything over 4 days old
• Clean shared surfaces (counters, microwaves, coffee stations) before and after use
• Wash hands before handling food — break room surfaces are among the highest-touch areas in any workplace
• If food doesn't smell or look right, don't eat it — foodborne illness from spoiled food is not worth the risk
Did You Know Stat: Office break room kitchen sinks contain more bacteria than workplace restrooms, on average. Shared appliance handles and refrigerator door seals are among the highest contamination points. (NSF International)
Discussion Prompt: When did you last clean out your shared refrigerator? Are there written expectations in your workplace about shared kitchen cleanliness?

Title: Smoke Detectors and CO Alarms
Summary: Smoke detectors and carbon monoxide alarms save lives — but only if they're working. Testing, maintaining, and responding correctly to these devices is a responsibility for every workplace and home.
Key Points:
• Test smoke alarms and CO detectors monthly using the test button; replace batteries annually
• Replace smoke alarms every 10 years and CO detectors every 5-7 years (check the manufacturer's date)
• Never disable or cover a smoke alarm because of nuisance alarms — address the source of false triggers instead
• When an alarm sounds: treat it as real, evacuate immediately, and call 911 — don't investigate first
• Interconnected alarms (when one sounds, all sound) provide significantly better protection in larger facilities
Did You Know Stat: Three of every five home fire deaths occur in homes with no smoke alarms or with non-working alarms. Working smoke alarms cut the risk of dying in a fire by 50%. (NFPA/CDC)
Discussion Prompt: When were the smoke and CO detectors in your workplace last tested? Do you know where all the detectors are in your work area?

Title: Electrical Safety Basics
Summary: Electrical hazards are present in virtually every workplace, but most people have little formal training in recognizing them. A few fundamental rules dramatically reduce risk from electrical shock and fire.
Key Points:
• Never use a damaged cord — frayed insulation, bent plugs, or missing ground pins should mean immediate replacement
• Extension cords are temporary devices — never use them as permanent wiring or daisy-chain them together
• Do not overload outlets or power strips — too many high-draw appliances on one circuit is a fire risk
• Respect electrical panel access — only qualified personnel should open them; never block access to panels
• If an outlet sparks, feels warm, or trips repeatedly, report it to facilities — don't reset and ignore
Did You Know Stat: Electrical fires account for approximately 51,000 home fires, 500 deaths, and $1.3 billion in property damage each year. Extension cord misuse is among the leading causes. (ESFI/CPSC)
Discussion Prompt: Are there any extension cords in your workspace being used as permanent wiring? Any outlets or power strips that feel warm or trip frequently?

Title: Home Office and Remote Work Ergonomics
Source Reference: OSHA-3123 / NIOSH / CDC Total Worker Health
Summary: Remote and hybrid workers are not immune to ergonomic injuries — and working from kitchen tables, couches, and makeshift setups often creates worse conditions than a properly equipped office. The investment in a good setup pays off quickly.
Key Points:
• Avoid working from couches, beds, or hunched over a laptop on a low surface for extended periods
• A laptop stand and external keyboard/mouse are low-cost changes that dramatically improve posture
• Your home office chair should support your lower back; a rolled towel or pillow can substitute for lumbar support
• Natural light is beneficial, but avoid having windows or bright lights directly behind your monitor (glare) or behind you (screen reflection)
• Establish a clear end-of-workday routine — blurring work and home time is a leading cause of remote worker burnout
Did You Know Stat: Remote workers report higher rates of neck and back pain than office workers, largely attributed to unsuitable home workstation setups. Ergonomic equipment has an estimated 17:1 return on investment. (OSHA/Cornell University)
Discussion Prompt: If you work from home, have you ever had a formal assessment of your home workstation? What's the weakest part of your home setup?

Title: Medication Safety at Work
Source Reference: NIOSH / DOT Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse / SAMHSA
Summary: Medications — including common over-the-counter drugs — can affect alertness, reaction time, and judgment in ways that matter for workplace safety. Being aware of these effects and knowing what to do about them is everyone's responsibility.
Key Points:
• Many common medications cause drowsiness, dizziness, or impaired coordination — read the label for warnings before safety-sensitive tasks
• If a medication affects your ability to do your job safely, inform your supervisor — you won't be disciplined for disclosing a medical need
• Never take someone else's prescription medication, even for a common complaint — dosing, interactions, and contraindications vary
• Store medications securely at work — leaving prescription medications in open areas creates theft and misuse risk
• If you are in recovery, know your organization's EAP resources — they are confidential and exist to support you
Did You Know Stat: Approximately 70% of the estimated 14.8 million Americans who use illicit drugs are employed. Impaired workers are 3.6 times more likely to be involved in a workplace accident. (SAMHSA/NIOSH)
Discussion Prompt: Have you ever worked while taking a medication that made you drowsy or lightheaded? Did you adjust your tasks or workload that day?

Title: Back Care and Spine Health
Source Reference: NIOSH Publication 97-141 / OSHA Back Injury Prevention
Summary: Low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide and the most common musculoskeletal complaint in every type of workplace. Most back injuries are not caused by a single dramatic event, but by cumulative small stresses over time.
Key Points:
• The lumbar spine is most vulnerable when bent forward and twisted simultaneously — avoid combined bending and twisting whenever possible
• Core strength is your spine's best protection — regular strengthening (planks, bridges) reduces back injury risk significantly
• Adjust your car seat, chair, and workstation so you can maintain the natural 'S' curve of your spine
• When pain begins, early movement (gentle walking, stretching) is generally better than rest for most back conditions
• Chronic back pain is often linked to stress, poor sleep, and sedentary behavior — addressing these helps
Did You Know Stat: Low back pain affects approximately 80% of Americans at some point in their lives and is the most common cause of job-related disability. U.S. costs exceed $100 billion annually. (NIOSH/BLS)
Discussion Prompt: Do you experience back discomfort during or after your workday? Have you had your workstation or job tasks reviewed for back hazards?

Title: Office Fire Prevention
Summary: Office fires are more common than many people think — and most are preventable. Electrical overloads, unattended heat sources, and cluttered storage areas are the most frequent contributors.
Key Points:
• Never leave space heaters unattended or running overnight — they are among the top causes of office fires
• Keep space heaters at least 3 feet from paper, fabric, and other combustibles
• Don't overload power strips — high-draw appliances (heaters, microwaves, coffee makers) need dedicated circuits
• Keep storage rooms and electrical closets uncluttered — blocked panels and piled paper near heat sources are serious hazards
• Ensure exit paths and fire extinguisher access are never blocked, even temporarily
Did You Know Stat: Office and store fires cause an estimated $112 million in property damage annually. Electrical distribution equipment and intentional fires are the leading causes; space heaters are a significant contributor. (NFPA)
Discussion Prompt: Are there any space heaters in your area? Are they approved by facilities, and are they turned off at the end of the day?

Title: Fall Protection at Six Feet
Summary: Falls are the leading cause of death in construction. At 6 feet or more above a lower level, fall protection is the law, not a judgment call. Name your protection before you climb.
Key Points:
• Any unprotected side or edge, hole, or leading edge 6 feet or more above a lower level needs guardrails, safety nets, or a personal fall arrest system — there is no exception for a quick task
• Guardrails need a top rail around 42 inches, a midrail, and the strength to hold 200 pounds — report damaged or missing sections immediately
• Use a full-body harness (body belts don't count) with the lanyard attached to an anchorage rated for 5,000 pounds per worker — inspect your gear before every use
• Guard or cover every floor hole and skylight — covers must be able to hold the loads they'll see and be labeled as covers
• Wear your hard hat whenever work is happening overhead — falling object protection is part of the same rule
Did You Know Stat: In 2024, 389 of 1,034 construction deaths were falls to a lower level — the industry's leading cause of death. (OSHA/BLS)
Discussion Prompt: Point at the nearest edge 6 feet up — what is protecting the person working there today?

Title: Scaffold Safety Basics
Summary: Scaffolds put crews at height on a platform someone built this week. A competent person must inspect the scaffold every shift; your job is to use it the way it was built.
Key Points:
• A competent person inspects the scaffold before each shift and after anything that could shake it — no tag, no climb
• Platforms are fully planked with gaps under an inch — no missing planks, and no boxes or ladders stacked on top to gain height
• Frame scaffolds taller than 4-to-1 (height to base width) must be tied, guyed, or braced, and rest on base plates and mud sills
• Fall protection kicks in above 10 feet on scaffolds — guardrails or a harness, every time
• Never climb the cross braces, and keep 10 feet away from overhead power lines
Did You Know Stat: OSHA's Stop Falls campaign exists because falls from ladders, scaffolds, and roofs are the leading cause of death in construction. (OSHA)
Discussion Prompt: Who inspected our scaffold this morning, and what would you do if the tag were missing?

Title: Trenching and Excavation Safety
Summary: A trench wall is a wall of dirt that can weigh more than a car per cubic yard. Slope it, shore it, or shield it — the ground doesn't give second chances.
Key Points:
• Cave-in protection (sloping or benching, shoring, or a trench box) is required at 5 feet and deeper — a shallower trench is entered only if a competent person examined the soil and cleared it
• The competent person inspects every day before work starts, after every rainstorm, and as conditions change — nobody enters a trench on their own say-so
• A ladder, ramp, or stairway must be within 25 feet of everyone inside a trench 4 feet or deeper
• Keep spoil piles and equipment at least 2 feet back from the edge
• Never stand under a load handled by digging or lifting equipment, and stay out of trench boxes while they are being moved
Did You Know Stat: Cave-ins killed 80 U.S. workers in 2024, and OSHA warns trench collapses are more likely than other excavation incidents to be fatal. (BLS CFOI 2024; OSHA Alert 3971)
Discussion Prompt: Name our competent person for today's dig — when did they last walk the trench?

Title: Struck-By Hazards on the Jobsite
Summary: Struck-by is one of OSHA's Construction Focus Four: hit by vehicles, equipment, swinging loads, or objects falling from above. Every struck-by event has a line of fire — your job is to never stand in it.
Key Points:
• Never walk or work under a suspended load or anything handled by lifting or digging equipment
• Make eye contact with equipment operators before crossing in front of machines — assume they can't see you
• Wear high-visibility gear near public traffic and stay inside barriers or warning systems near excavation edges
• Hard hats stay on anywhere work is happening overhead
• Stack and secure materials so nothing rolls, slides, or falls onto the crew below
Did You Know Stat: Struck by a propelled, falling, or suspended object killed 357 U.S. workers in 2024. (BLS CFOI)
Discussion Prompt: If that excavator swung right now, where would you be? Pick your escape route.

Title: Caught-In/Between Hazards
Summary: Caught-in/between is one of OSHA's Construction Focus Four: being pinned between equipment and a wall, pulled into an unguarded moving part, or buried in a collapse. Machines don't pinch — they crush.
Key Points:
• Keep hands, feet, and clothing out of rotating parts, pulleys, and pinch points — guards exist because body parts don't survive contact
• Never reach into running equipment to clear a jam — shut it down and lock it out first
• Stay clear of equipment swing radii and never position yourself between moving equipment and a fixed object
• Never enter an unprotected trench — cave-ins are caught-in/between too
• Stand away from vehicles being loaded or unloaded
Did You Know Stat: Struck, caught, or compressed by running powered equipment killed 213 U.S. workers in 2024. (BLS CFOI)
Discussion Prompt: Name one spot on this site where a person and a machine could meet — and how we make sure they never do.

Title: Electrical Safety on the Jobsite
Summary: Temporary power is the site's most convenient hazard. GFCIs, cord discipline, and respecting lockouts are what stand between 120 volts and a fatality.
Key Points:
• Every 120-volt temporary receptacle outlet is GFCI-protected — or on a documented assured-grounding program
• Inspect cords and plugs before each day's use — damaged, cut, or missing-ground cords get removed, not taped
• Only authorized people lock out and tag circuits — a locked-out circuit restarts for nobody
• Treat every wire as live until proven dead
• Keep ladders, scaffolds, and tools at least 10 feet from overhead power lines
Did You Know Stat: Exposure to electricity killed 130 U.S. workers in 2024. (BLS CFOI)
Discussion Prompt: Is every cord on this job GFCI-protected — and when did you last actually look at one?

Title: Lockout/Tagout Basics
Summary: Machines don't know you're working on them. Lockout/tagout is how we make sure stored energy — electrical, hydraulic, pneumatic, gravity — can't move a machine while your hands are inside.
Key Points:
• Before service or maintenance: shut down, isolate every energy source, and apply your personal lock — one worker, one lock
• Lock, tag, try — after locking, try the start control to prove zero energy
• Only authorized workers lock out, and only the person who applied a lock removes it
• Never operate, bypass, or "just test" equipment that is locked or tagged out
• Circuits on this site follow the same rule — lock and tag before you touch
Did You Know Stat: Unexpected startup or release of stored energy can crush, amputate, burn, or kill — craft workers are among those at greatest risk. (OSHA)
Discussion Prompt: What machines here could start up or move while someone's hands are in them — and where are their locks?

Title: Machine Guards and Power Tools
Summary: Guards and interlocks are the difference between a close call and an amputation. A tool that has been tampered with isn't a shortcut — it's a hazard with a trigger.
Key Points:
• Guards stay on any power tool designed to have them — removing a guard puts skin against the blade
• Exposed moving parts — belts, pulleys, blades, sprockets — must be guarded, on bench tools and site equipment alike
• Circular saws, reciprocating saws, and percussion tools must have a constant-pressure switch — the blade stops when your finger does
• Inspect tools before use — damaged tools get tagged out and taken out of service
• Wear eye and face protection whenever chips, sparks, or dust can fly
Did You Know Stat: 756 U.S. workers died in contact incidents in 2024 — struck by, or caught in or compressed by, objects and powered equipment. (BLS CFOI)
Discussion Prompt: Find one guard on this site that has been defeated or removed — what would it take to fix it today?

Title: Aerial Lift Safety
Summary: Boom lifts and scissor lifts get work done fast at height — and tip, crush, and drop people just as fast when the daily rules get skipped.
Key Points:
• Test the lift controls each day before use — only authorized, trained operators run the lift
• Stand on the basket floor — never climb the rails, and never stand on planks or ladders inside the basket
• Wear a harness with the lanyard attached to the boom or basket — never tie off to a pole, structure, or anything outside the lift
• Respect the manufacturer's load limit — people, tools, and material all count
• Set the brakes, use outrigger pads on solid ground, chock on inclines, and never drive with the boom raised unless the lift is designed for it
Did You Know Stat: Falls to a lower level killed 666 U.S. workers in 2024 — lift work is height work, and the rules apply. (BLS CFOI)
Discussion Prompt: Who ran the morning control check on our lift, and where is their lanyard anchored?

Title: Jobsite Housekeeping
Summary: Construction sites change hourly — and yesterday's tidy site is today's obstacle course. Housekeeping is the cheapest safety fix there is: it's free, and it's everyone's job.
Key Points:
• Clear form and scrap lumber — especially with protruding nails — from work areas, passageways, and stairs as work moves
• Pull or bend down every exposed nail before lumber gets stacked or walked past
• Remove combustible scrap regularly and keep waste and oily-rag containers emptied — fire loads grow fast on site
• Keep walkways, stairs, and access routes lit and clear — night shifts and winter afternoons make clutter deadly
• A tidy site is an inspected site — most hazards you'll find while cleaning up are ones an inspector would write up too
Did You Know Stat: Falls, slips, and trips killed 844 U.S. workers in 2024 — most start with something in the way. (BLS CFOI)
Discussion Prompt: What's one thing we can clear from our walkways before the next shift starts?
